extracted.intended_audience: journalists, photo editors, and the general public interested in media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing and publishing news photographs, emphasizing authenticity, proper vetting, and editorial responsibility when digital tools and competitive pressures create temptation to manipulate images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic authenticity / no deceptive digital alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers should not digitally alter pictures in ways that change the meaning or content of the scene (i.e., 'doctoring' images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives examples (Adnan Hajj, Brian Walski) where alteration led to termination and removal of photos from databases. It frames such doctoring as unethical and unacceptable in news journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper vetting procedures for images
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should have and increase procedures to vet images properly before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance: 'This should be a clarion call to media companies to increase their procedures in vetting images properly,' (Kenny Irby, Poynter Institute). The article implies organizations must verify authenticity before use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish acceptable edits from deceptive manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that many news photos undergo some form of digital alteration, but distinguish routine/clarifying edits from alterations that mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes 'Nearly all news photographs undergo some form of digital alteration these days' — implying a need for editorial policy to define permissible post-processing vs prohibited doctoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating composites or merged images that misrepresent events
rubrics_metrics.description: Merging separate images (e.g., different people/instances) to create a single misleading scene is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Brian Walski was fired in 2003 for merging two images so it appeared a soldier was pointing at a man holding a child. Such composites that alter factual meaning are unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility: do not sacrifice scrutiny for speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must balance competitive pressure and timeliness with the need for rigorous checking of images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article warns that 'growing pressure in newsrooms to compete... may tempt photographers to push ethical boundaries and editors to sacrifice scrutiny for speed,' highlighting the need for policies that prioritize verification even under deadline pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and corrective action when manipulation is discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: When a doctored image is discovered, organizations should take corrective actions such as removing images and terminating relationships if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Reuters example: once blogger scrutiny exposed doctored photos, Reuters terminated its relationship with the photographer and pulled his work from the database — illustrating expected accountability measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: External/public scrutiny as a verification mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The blogosphere and public scrutiny can play a role in detecting doctored images and prompting corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article credits blogger Charles Johnson of Little Green Footballs with first sounding the alarm about Hajj's doctored photos, showing how outside observers can augment internal vetting.
